questions.question: You need one lookup in a small unsorted array. Which choice has the best justification?
options: Sort, then binary search, because log n is always smallest
Use linear search and avoid sorting preparation
Use merge sort and stop halfway
Use selection sort because it makes few swaps
questions.explanation: One O(n) scan is normally cheaper than O(n log n) preparation for a single logarithmic lookup.
optionFeedback: This ignores the sorting cost and the small number of searches.
Correct: linear search matches the current data and operation.
A partial merge sort does not perform a valid search.
Selection sort does not locate the key and still costs quadratic comparisons.

questions.question: Which taught sort best fits a large unpredictable array when O(n) temporary memory is allowed and a quadratic worst case is unacceptable?
questions.explanation: Merge sort provides O(n log n) worst-case time and uses O(n) auxiliary array space.
optionFeedback: Bubble sort has a quadratic worst case.
Selection sort remains quadratic in every input order.
Insertion sort can be quadratic on unpredictable data.
Correct: the scenario accepts merge sort's memory cost in exchange for the guaranteed bound.

questions.question: What does stability preserve?
options: The original relative order of records with equal keys
questions.explanation: Stable sorting keeps equal-key records in the order they had before the sort.
optionFeedback: Every correct sort preserves the number of elements; that is not stability.
Correct: stability concerns equal-key relative order.
Stable algorithms can have different time complexities.
Stability does not require a fixed swap count.

questions.question: Selection changes [2A,2B,1] into [1,2B,2A]. What does this show?
options: The taught selection sort is not stable
questions.explanation: Tagged equal-key records have reversed their original order.
optionFeedback: Correct: labels expose the instability.
Numerically 1,2,2 is sorted.
The swap does not establish recursion.
This swap needs only constant extra storage.

questions.question: Six swaps write two array cells each. How many array writes are counted, excluding the local temp?
questions.explanation: Count two destination array assignments per swap.
optionFeedback: That counts swaps rather than array writes.
Correct: six times two gives twelve.
That includes a temp assignment excluded by this convention.
This is not the requested write count.

questions.question: Which demand conflicts with all four taught array sorts?
options: Large unpredictable input with buffer allowed
Stable, constant-extra-space, O(n log n) worst-case sort
Sorted input with bubble early stop
questions.explanation: The simple sorts have quadratic worst cases; the taught merge implementation needs O(n) buffer storage.
optionFeedback: Insertion fits this scenario.
Merge fits these stated constraints.
Correct: no taught version meets every demand.
Optimized bubble fits a no-swap early-stop case.

questions.question: What is the growth-term cost of sorting once then making q binary lookups in retained sorted data?
options: n log n + q log n
questions.explanation: Include one preparation cost and q logarithmic searches.
optionFeedback: This omits the sort.
This charges sorting for every lookup.
The workflow is not a single logarithm.
Correct: preparation plus repeated lookups.

questions.question: Why can insertion benefit from nearly sorted input?
questions.explanation: Key movement depends on how far each key lies from its correct position.
optionFeedback: Correct: local disorder causes limited movement.
Each pass still checks the key.
The taught method uses constant extra storage.
Reverse input still has quadratic movement.

questions.question: What does peak auxiliary space for recursive array merge count?
options: O(n) live temporary storage plus O(log n) frames
Every allocation accumulated for the entire run
Constant storage independent of input size
questions.explanation: Space complexity counts simultaneously live extra storage, excluding the original input.
optionFeedback: Auxiliary storage excludes the supplied array.
Correct: distinguish buffer peak and live stack depth.
Cumulative allocation volume is a different measure.
The merge buffer grows with n.

questions.question: Changing strict > to >= in insertion's record comparison can lose which property?
options: The need for a saved key
questions.explanation: An equal earlier record may shift past the newly inserted equal record.
optionFeedback: Sorting preserves array length either way.
The index still decreases toward termination.
Correct: equal records can cross.
Shifts can still overwrite the original cell, so save the key.
